what: White Mountains Insurance is a holding company that buys and builds insurance and financial businesses. It owns specialty insurance operations, a bermudian reinsurer, a mortgage insurance business in Europe, and stakes in various financial companies, and it sells them when the price is right.
customers: Varies by subsidiary: insurance brokers and policyholders across specialty lines, European mortgage lenders, and the various end markets of the businesses it holds.
money: Premiums earned across its specialty insurance and reinsurance subsidiaries.
Earnings from non-insurance holdings and investment returns on the float.
moat: The model is disciplined capital allocation rather than any single operating advantage: buy insurance businesses at sensible prices, let them underwrite carefully, invest the premium float, and sell when someone pays more than the business is worth. Insurance float is capital held before claims are paid, which can be invested for the holder’s benefit in the meantime.
risks: No analyst coverage is reflected in the data, so there is no external check on the valuation at all.
The value depends almost entirely on management’s capital allocation judgement, which cannot be assessed from outside in any given year.
Earnings are lumpy because they include gains on selling businesses, which makes any single year’s figures misleading.
Revenue swung from $614.4M in 2021 to $3.7B in 2025 as the portfolio changed, so the revenue line describes acquisitions rather than performance.
Insurance underwriting can produce large losses from catastrophes, and reinsurance concentrates that exposure.
opportunities: Trailing net income of $944.5M on $3.6B of revenue, with the shares at about 5.9 times earnings and 4.9 times EV/EBITDA.
Last year’s net margin was 29.6%, and free cash flow was $385.5M.
Debt of $893.2M is modest relative to the asset base.
A long record of buying insurance businesses well and selling them at good prices is the only thing this model requires.
Insurance float provides investable capital at low or negative cost when underwriting is disciplined.
watch: Book value per share over time. For a holding company of this kind, the growth in book value per share is the only meaningful measure of whether management is creating value.
view: White Mountains is a capital allocation vehicle wearing an insurance company’s clothes, and it should be judged accordingly. It buys insurance and financial businesses, lets them underwrite, invests the premium float, and sells them when somebody offers more than they are worth. That is the Berkshire model at a much smaller scale, and like Berkshire it cannot be analysed from the income statement, because the earnings include gains on disposals and therefore lurch from year to year.

The only honest measure for a company like this is book value per share compounded over long periods. Revenue swinging from $614 million in 2021 to $3.7 billion in 2025 tells you the portfolio changed, not that the business improved. Trailing net income of $944 million at 5.9 times earnings looks extraordinarily cheap and may well include a disposal gain that does not repeat. Neither figure should drive a decision.

What makes the model work when it works is insurance float: premiums are collected before claims are paid, and that money can be invested in the meantime. If the underwriting roughly breaks even, the float is free investable capital, and compounding free capital is how these vehicles create value over decades. If underwriting loses money, the float has a cost and the whole structure becomes much less attractive. Underwriting discipline is therefore the hinge, and it is the first thing to check.

What makes this hard to own is the complete absence of external scrutiny — the data shows no analyst coverage at all, on a $5.3 billion company trading at $2,210 a share. Nobody is checking the assumptions, and the share price alone makes it inaccessible to most investors. That can mean genuine mispricing or it can mean nobody has found a reason to look. Either way, this requires trusting management’s judgement over a long period, and the only evidence that matters is the book value per share record.
bull: Disciplined underwriting generates low-cost float, management keeps buying insurance businesses well and selling them high, and book value per share compounds unexamined.
bear: A capital allocation decision goes wrong or a catastrophe hits the reinsurance book, and with no analyst coverage the problem is invisible until it is reported.
